question: Who are wiser, the children of this world or the children of light?
summary: Luke 16:8 has Jesus declare, in the parable of the unjust steward, that "the children of this world are in their generation wiser than the children of light." James 3:15-17 contrasts earthly, sensual, devilish wisdom with the wisdom from above, valorizing the wisdom of those aligned with God. The Lukan saying gives the wisdom-edge to worldly people; James gives it to the heavenly-minded.

reconcile.connective: Commentators read Luke's "wiser" as shrewdness confined to worldly self-interest, not the God-ward piety James calls true wisdom from above.

discrepancy.connective: Steve Wells's Skeptic's Annotated Bible frames it as a flat contradiction: Jesus commends worldly cunning, James condemns that very wisdom as devilish.

skeptic.name: Steve Wells
skeptic.attribution: Steve Wells, Skeptic's Annotated Bible (1999), contra/wiser.html

pd_work.resource: Jamieson, Fausset & Brown, Commentary Critical and Explanatory on the Whole Bible (1871), on Luke 16:8
pd_work.author: Jamieson, Fausset & Brown
pd_work.note: JFB reads Luke's 'wiser' as a narrower shrewdness in 'adaptation of means to ends,' explicitly denying it concerns 'God and eternity' — the same distinction James draws between earthly and heavenly wisdom. John Haley's Examination of the Alleged Discrepancies of the Bible (1874) was checked (curl+grep of the full djvu text): it independently quotes James 3:15 against James 3:17 verbatim under its 'Wisdom' heading and resolves it by distinguishing 'worldly craft' from 'enlightened piety,' but does not address the Luke 16:8 side of this pairing by name, so JFB — keyed to the actual passage in tension — is used as the primary defense source.

excerpts.excerpt_text: The greater wisdom (or shrewdness) of the one, in adaptation of means to ends, and in energetic, determined prosecution of them, is none of it for God and eternity—a region they were never in, an atmosphere they never breathed, an undiscovered world, an unborn existence to them—but all for the purposes of their own grovelling and fleeting generation.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Distinguishes Luke's 'wiser' as a narrow worldly shrewdness explicitly not 'for God and eternity' — the same axis James uses to separate earthly from heavenly wisdom.
excerpts.source_note_text:
the lord--evidently the steward's lord, so called in Luk 16:3, Luk 16:5.
commended, &c.--not for his "injustice," but "because he had done wisely," or prudently; with commendable foresight and skilful adaptation of means to end.
children of this world--so Luk 20:34; compare Psa 17:14 ("their portion in this life"); Phi 3:19 ("mind earthly things"); Psa 4:6-7.
their generation--or "for their generation"--that is, for the purposes of the "world" they are "of." The greater wisdom (or shrewdness) of the one, in adaptation of means to ends, and in energetic, determined prosecution of them, is none of it for God and eternity--a region they were never in, an atmosphere they never breathed, an undiscovered world, an unborn existence to them--but all for the purposes of their own grovelling and fleeting generation.
children of light--(so Joh 12:36; Eph 5:8; Th1 5:5). Yet this is only "as night-birds see better in the dark than those of the day owls than eagles" [CAJETAN and TRENCH]. But we may learn lessons from them, as our Lord now shows, and "be wise as serpents."
